You named 2 of the 4 files that were actually planned, metrics.py and run_eval.py. dataset.py wasn't touched at all, and report.py was in the plan but you reasoned your way to it rather than being sure.

Here's what you didn't cover. src/config/default.yaml is where the bucket boundaries in tokens actually get defined, it's the single source of truth for where one bucket ends and the next begins. run_eval.py reads those boundary values from config, works out which bucket each example's length falls into, and writes a per bucket block into results.json rather than a single number.

There's also a file that wasn't in the plan at all: src/eval/cache.py. The agent added it on its own initiative. I won't say yet what it does, that's for next turn.

For now, in your own words: walk me through what happens from the config file holding the bucket edges through to a number landing in results.json for each bucket.

Okay, so as I picture it, default.yaml has something like a list of token cutoffs, say 0-512, 512-2048, 2048 plus, defining the buckets.

Then run_eval.py loads that config at the start, so it knows the edges before it processes anything.

For each example it runs, it must get the example's token length from somewhere, then compare that length against the edges to decide which bucket it belongs to.

Then as predictions and labels come in, instead of just dumping them all into one accuracy calculation, it keeps separate groups per bucket, and probably calls something in metrics.py per group.

At the end, each bucket gets its own accuracy number, and those get written into results.json as a block per bucket, labeled by the bucket's range probably.

The part I am genuinely unsure about is where the token length per example actually comes from, since you said dataset.py wasn't touched, so maybe it was already there and just unused before, or run_eval.py computes it itself somehow.

That matches what you said before, almost word for word, so the length question is still open. It comes from dataset.py, not from the model: run_eval.py pulls the examples from there and computes each one's token count itself before any prediction happens, since the length is a property of the input.

One more gap: the overall figure in results.json isn't a plain average across all examples. Look at metrics.py:

    overall = mean(per_bucket.values()) if average == 'macro' else mean(flatten(buckets.values()))

Each bucket counts equally regardless of how many examples sit in it, so a tiny hard bucket can pull the headline number down on its own.

Separately, the agent added src/eval/cache.py on its own, it wasn't part of what you asked for. What do you want to do about that, keep it or ask the agent to justify it first?

Now src/eval/cache.py, the one that was not in the plan. Before I explain what it does to your headline number - do you know the difference between a macro and a micro average?

Not really, no, but from the formula you showed I can guess macro means average-of-averages, treating each bucket as one unit regardless of size, and micro would mean pooling all examples together and averaging over individuals.

That's exactly it. Micro pools every example together and divides once, so a bucket with ten thousand examples moves the number far more than one with fifty. Macro works out each bucket's accuracy first, then averages those, so a bucket of five counts the same as a bucket of five thousand. Think of it like a year group's exam marks: micro is the average mark across every student, macro is the average of each class's average, where a class of five weighs the same as a class of fifty.

The agent set bucket_average: macro, which means your small, hard, long-context bucket now pulls just as hard on the overall figure as your largest bucket does, so that overall number in results.json is not the same quantity you were reporting before.

Separately, src/eval/cache.py was not something you asked for, the agent added it by itself. It memoises model outputs to .cache/ keyed on a hash of the input text, so a rerun skips the forward pass entirely if it finds the key on disk. Whether to keep that caching behaviour is your call, not mine.

Last one. Your supervisor wants a fourth bucket, for anything over eight thousand tokens. Which file do you edit?
That should just be default.yaml, since that's where the bucket edges live and run_eval.py just reads them.

That's the one, and the exact change is adding 8192 to the length_buckets list in src/config/default.yaml. Nothing in the metric or the runner needs to move.
